code.title: fetch resolves on 404/500: check res.ok

followUps:
Look at the abort reason. A timeout made by AbortSignal.timeout(ms) rejects with a DOMException named TimeoutError; a manual controller.abort() rejects with AbortError.

So the catch block can branch on e.name: show "request took too long, retry?" for a timeout and show nothing for a user cancel. You can also call controller.abort('user') and read signal.reason to be explicit.

catch (e) {
  if (e.name === 'TimeoutError') showRetry();
  else if (e.name === 'AbortError') return; // user cancelled
  else throw e;
}

The second call fails, because a response body is a stream that can be read only once. It throws a TypeError such as "body stream already read".

If you need the body twice, call res.clone() before reading and read each copy once, or read once and keep the result. A related trap: if res.json() fails to parse, the body is already used up, so you cannot fall back to res.text(). Read text() once, then JSON.parse it inside a try block.

It looks like a plain, uninformative failure: fetch rejects with a TypeError ("Failed to fetch"), with no status code and no hint that CORS was the cause.

The browser hides the details on purpose so a page cannot probe other sites. The real reason (a missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, or a failed preflight) appears only in the devtools console. From code you cannot tell it apart from being offline. The fix is on the server by sending the correct headers; mode: 'no-cors' does not fix it, it only gives you an opaque response you cannot read.

Keep it in memory, in a plain JavaScript variable, and get a new one from a refresh token stored in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.

Memory is not readable by other scripts the way localStorage is, and the HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by script at all. The cost: on page reload the token is gone, so the app calls the refresh endpoint at start-up. Example: an access token valid for 10 minutes is refreshed shortly before it expires. This limits what a stolen script can take, but you still need CSP and XSS prevention.

The write fails and you must handle it: localStorage.setItem throws a QuotaExceededError, and an IndexedDB transaction aborts with the same error, rolling back its changes.

So wrap writes in try/catch, delete old or least-used data and retry, and tell the user if it still fails. You can check room beforehand with navigator.storage.estimate() (it returns usage and quota in bytes). By default storage is best-effort, so under disk pressure the browser may clear a whole origin; navigator.storage.persist() asks to protect it.

Through the storage event, which fires in the other tabs of the same origin whenever localStorage changes. It does not fire in the tab that made the change.

window.addEventListener('storage', e => {
  if (e.key === 'theme') apply(e.newValue); // oldValue is also given
});

For messages that are not stored data, such as "user logged out", a BroadcastChannel is cleaner: every tab on the same channel name receives what another tab posts.

code.title: Search-as-you-type: latest request wins

followUps:
Debounce comes first and abort comes second; they solve different problems and you normally use both.

Debounce decides whether to send a request at all: typing "cat" quickly produces one request after a 250 ms pause instead of three. Abort cleans up a request that was already sent: if the user types another letter while that request is in flight, you cancel it and send the new one. Debounce cuts the number of requests; abort (or a sequence check) guarantees an old response never replaces a newer one.

Keep a Map from the normalised query (trimmed, lower-cased) to its results, and look there before calling the network.

Example: the user types "ab", then backspaces to "a"; the results for "a" are in the map, so they appear instantly. Add a time limit per entry so data does not go stale, and a size limit: with a Map, delete and re-set the key on each hit, and when size passes 50 delete the oldest key (map.keys().next().value), which gives a simple LRU cache. You can show the cached results at once and refresh them in the background.

Yes, any screen where the latest user choice must win has the same race: if the user clicks page 3 and then page 4, a slow page 3 reply can arrive last and overwrite page 4.

Fix it the same way: abort the previous request when the page or tab changes, or tag each request with its key (query + page + tab) and render only if the key still matches the current state. Switching tabs can also keep a cache per tab so going back is instant. Be careful not to abort a "load more" append that you still want.

code.title: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

followUps:
A thundering herd is many clients doing the same thing at the same moment, for example all retrying a failed request at once, so the recovering server gets hit by a huge spike and fails again.

Example: 1,000 clients fail at 12:00:00 and all retry after exactly 1 second, so 1,000 requests land at 12:00:01. Exponential backoff plus random jitter (each client waits a random time up to the ceiling) spreads them out over the whole interval. Respecting a Retry-After header and capping attempts also helps.

A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, so you fail fast instead of waiting on timeouts. It has three states: closed (normal), open (reject immediately) and half-open (let one probe through).

  1. Count consecutive failures while closed.
  2. After 5 failures, go open for 30 seconds and fail every call at once.
  3. Then go half-open: one success closes the breaker, one failure reopens it.
if (state === 'open' && now < reopenAt) throw new Error('circuit open');
try { const r = await call(); fails = 0; state = 'closed'; return r; }
catch (e) { if (++fails >= 5) { state = 'open'; reopenAt = now + 30000; } throw e; }

Usually yes, because fetch resolves as soon as the headers arrive, and the body can still stall or download slowly afterwards.

If you use one AbortSignal.timeout(ms) signal and do not clear it when the headers arrive, it stays active while you call res.json(), and the body read rejects too when time runs out. If you call clearTimeout right after fetch resolves, the body is unprotected. For large downloads, use a longer total limit or an idle timeout (reset on every chunk) instead of one short limit.

It means the callback runs each time the visible fraction of the element crosses 0%, 50% or 100%.

Example: a 200 px tall image scrolls into view. You get a call when the first pixel shows (ratio 0), another when 100 px are visible (0.5), and another when all 200 px are visible (1), and again on the way out in reverse. Read entry.intersectionRatio to see which crossing it was. A single number such as 0.5 means only that one crossing, and the default 0 fires when any pixel enters or the last pixel leaves.

Because 100% visible is not always reachable: an element taller than the root (for example a 1200 px block in a 800 px viewport) can never be fully inside it.

It also never reaches 1 if an ancestor with overflow: hidden clips it, or if fractional pixels (zoom, scaling) make the ratio 0.99. Use a smaller threshold such as 0.9, or for tall elements use 0 and compute the visible part yourself. Remember the callback also fires once right after observe with the starting state.

Pass the scrolling element as the root option; by default root is null, which means the browser viewport.

const io = new IntersectionObserver(cb, {
  root: document.querySelector('#list'), // the scrolling box
  rootMargin: '0px 0px 200px 0px', threshold: 0
});

The root must be an ancestor of the observed targets, and rootMargin grows or shrinks that root box, so a positive bottom margin starts loading before the user reaches the end.

code.title: Infinite scroll: loading guard, cursor, hasMore

followUps:
Because offset pagination breaks when the data changes between requests, while a cursor always means "continue after this exact item".

Example: page size 20, you have shown items 1-20. A new item is inserted at the top, so the old item 20 moves to position 21 and offset 20 returns it again, a duplicate. A delete causes a skipped item. Cursors also scale better: the database seeks by index instead of counting past N rows.

SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id < :cursor
ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

Remember the scroll height before inserting, then move the scroll position by the amount that was added so the same item stays under the user's eyes.

const before = box.scrollHeight;
box.prepend(...newNodes);
box.scrollTop += box.scrollHeight - before;

Example: 5 new items add 300 px, so scrollTop grows by 300. Without this the view jumps to the new top. Browsers also have overflow-anchor scroll anchoring, which does some of this automatically; check that it works in your layout.

Keep the logic in a plain function that gets its dependencies passed in, and replace the browser parts with fakes.

Write loadMore(fetchPage) with no DOM calls, pass a fake fetchPage that returns scripted pages, and use a fake IntersectionObserver class that stores its callback so the test can trigger it by hand. Then assert: three rapid triggers cause one fetch, the last page sets hasMore to false, and after a failed fetch the next trigger retries. Use fake timers for delays, or jsdom if you need real DOM nodes.

So that many changes made in one go are grouped into a single call, instead of running your code in the middle of every individual change.

Appending 100 nodes in a loop gives one callback with an array of 100 records, run as a microtask right after your script ends and before the browser paints. The old synchronous mutation events fired 100 times, interrupting the code that made the change, which was slow and hard to reason about. Records can be read together and you can handle them in one pass.

The warning means the callback changed the size of an observed element, which would trigger another resize in the same frame, so the browser postponed the remaining notifications to the next frame.

Example: you observe a box and in the callback set its height from its width, so the size changes again. It is usually harmless, but it signals a possible loop. Avoid changing the observed element's own size in the callback, change a different element, or wrap the change in requestAnimationFrame.

Mutation events (DOMNodeInserted, DOMSubtreeModified and similar) were replaced by MutationObserver.

The old events were synchronous, fired for every single change, bubbled through the tree and were slow, and browsers deprecated them and are removing them. MutationObserver batches the records, delivers them asynchronously, and lets you choose exactly what to watch (childList, attributes, characterData, subtree) so you pay only for what you need.

When the work takes only a few milliseconds, or when copying the data costs more than the calculation.

A worker needs its script loaded and started, and every message is copied with structured clone. Sorting 100 numbers takes microseconds, so the message round trip is slower than doing it directly. A worker also cannot touch the DOM, so UI work stays on the main thread. A rule of thumb: move work off the main thread when it creates tasks longer than about 50 ms, or run it in chunks if it is small and frequent.

A Service Worker is an event-driven script that sits between your pages and the network for a whole origin, while a dedicated worker belongs to one page and exists to compute things.

A Service Worker intercepts fetch requests, so it can cache responses for offline use, receive push messages and run background sync. It is shared by all tabs of the site and the browser can stop it when it is idle, so it must not keep state in memory. Neither type can access the DOM.

Create a fixed number of workers, keep a queue of tasks, and give the next task to whichever worker becomes idle.

  1. Start N workers, usually navigator.hardwareConcurrency - 1.
  2. Each task gets an id and a promise; push it to the queue.
  3. When a worker is free, postMessage the next task to it.
  4. On its reply, resolve that id's promise and hand out the next task.
  5. On an error, reject the task and replace the worker; terminate all on unmount.

code.title: Client-side router: pattern matching with params and query

followUps:
Because popstate only fires when the user navigates (Back, Forward) or code calls history.go(); pushState just changes the URL and the history list.

The browser assumes that since your own code called pushState, it already knows about the change and will update the page itself. So a router wraps both steps:

function navigate(path) {
  history.pushState({}, '', path);
  render(path); // you must render yourself
}
addEventListener('popstate', () => render(location.pathname));

Hash routing (/#/users/1) works on any static host with no server setup, but the URLs are uglier and clash with in-page anchors. History routing gives clean URLs, but the server must serve index.html for every route.

With a hash, the part after # is never sent to the server, so refreshing always loads the one file. With history URLs, refreshing /users/1 asks the server for that path, and without a fallback rule you get a 404. Clean URLs also work better with server rendering and search engines.

Normalise the path before matching, and remove the base path first. Decide on one canonical form (usually no trailing slash) and treat the other as the same route.

let path = location.pathname.slice(BASE.length); // BASE = '/app'
if (path.length > 1 && path.endsWith('/')) {
  path = path.slice(0, -1);
  history.replaceState({}, '', BASE + path);
}

When creating links and calling pushState, add BASE back so /users/42/ and /users/42 both land on the same route under /app.

It stops the browser from sending the cookie on requests started by another site, except for ordinary top-level link clicks.

With Lax, the cookie is not sent for a hidden form POST, an image, an iframe or a fetch that a page on evil.com triggers, which blocks the usual CSRF attack. It is still sent when the user clicks a link to your site (a GET navigation). Strict blocks that too. Note that "same site" means the same registrable domain, so subdomains count as same site, and GET requests that change data are still unsafe.

Tell every tab at once, and make the server revoke the session so no tab can renew it.

With the token in memory, each tab holds its own copy, so on logout call the server to invalidate the refresh token (and clear the cookie), then broadcast the event:

const ch = new BroadcastChannel('auth');
ch.postMessage('logout');
ch.onmessage = e => { if (e.data === 'logout') clearAndRedirect(); };

The storage event on a localStorage key is a fallback for older browsers.

Token rotation means every use of a refresh token returns a new refresh token and makes the old one invalid, so a stolen token can be used at most once.

Example: an attacker copies token R1. The real user refreshes and receives R2, so R1 is now dead. If the attacker presents R1, the server sees an already-used token, concludes it was stolen and revokes the whole token family, forcing everyone to log in again. It shortens the damage window, but it does not replace preventing XSS.

Collect it from real users with the web-vitals library (onINP) or a PerformanceObserver on event entries, send it with navigator.sendBeacon to your analytics, and look at the 75th percentile.

INP is roughly the slowest interaction on the page: input delay plus handler time plus the time until the next paint. A value of 200 ms or less is considered good. Group results by page and device type, because a trace on your fast laptop will not show the problem a low-end phone has. Chrome's public field data (CrUX) gives a baseline.

Do the heavy work once in one place and let every tab read the result, instead of parsing the file in each tab.

Options: a SharedWorker, which all same-origin tabs can connect to; or parse in one tab (use the Web Locks API so only one tab does it), write the result to IndexedDB, and notify the others with a BroadcastChannel message that only says "dataset 17 is ready". Avoid sending large data over the channel, because it is copied to every tab.

There is no fixed limit; the cost grows with size, because structured clone copies the data and the time is spent on both the sending and receiving thread.

A few KB is free, but a very large object graph (hundreds of thousands of rows) can block the thread for noticeable milliseconds, which defeats the purpose. Measure with the Performance panel. For binary data, transfer an ArrayBuffer with postMessage(buf, [buf]), which moves it without copying, and for rows send pages or chunks instead of everything at once.

Open the database with a higher version number, and in onupgradeneeded run each migration step whose version is newer than event.oldVersion.

const req = indexedDB.open('app', 2);
req.onupgradeneeded = e => {
  const db = req.result;
  if (e.oldVersion < 1) db.createObjectStore('notes', { keyPath: 'id' });
  if (e.oldVersion < 2) req.transaction.objectStore('notes').createIndex('by_date', 'date');
};

Using < checks means a user who skips from version 0 to 2 runs both steps in order. Data fixes use the same upgrade transaction.

The key path is the property that serves as the primary key of an object store; an index is an extra lookup structure on another property.

Example: a store of users with keyPath: 'id' lets you do get(42). To find a user by email you create createIndex('by_email', 'email', { unique: true }) and call store.index('by_email').get('a@example.com'). A store has exactly one key (unique), but it can have many indexes, and an index may allow duplicates.

The request fails with a QuotaExceededError and the whole transaction aborts, so none of its changes are saved (all or nothing).

The onabort handler (or the rejected promise in a wrapper) is where you recover: free space by deleting old or least-recently-used records, then retry the transaction. You can reduce surprises by checking navigator.storage.estimate() before large writes. Because it is atomic, you never end up with half of a batch stored.

code.title: Data layer: in-flight dedupe plus TTL cache

followUps:
Put the user id into every cache key, and wipe all user-specific state when logging out.

On logout: abort in-flight requests, clear the in-memory cache, delete the IndexedDB data and the offline outbox, and ignore any late response by checking a session id that you stored when the request started. Example: key ['user', 17, 'orders'] never collides with ['user', 18, 'orders']. Per-user database names are an extra safety net.

Attach to every queued write the version it was based on, let the server detect a clash, and decide the resolution rule in advance.

Each outbox item has an idempotency key (so a replay does not create a duplicate) and the ETag or version it started from. If the server answers 409 or 412, apply a rule: last-write-wins for simple fields, field-level merge, or ask the user. Example: offline you rename a task to "A", a colleague renames it to "B"; the replay carries version 3 but the server is at 4, so you get a conflict.

For static assets, the app shell and offline pages, and for shared read-only caching that must work before your page code runs and across all tabs.

A Service Worker can precache the JavaScript and CSS, serve images cache-first, and answer public GET requests with stale-while-revalidate. It is a poor place for user-specific data and complicated invalidation rules, because it is hard to inspect and update; keep that logic in the app's own data layer. It is also the place for push messages and background sync.
